claims.text: Limited diffusion after casting produces a metastable state in a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEA.
The as-cast Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd alloy contains mixed solid-solution regions and metastable intermetallic phases.
Controlled post-casting annealing induces diffusion-driven phase partitioning and reordering.
Annealing causes Al, Gd, and possibly Cu to segregate to grain boundaries and interphase regions.
Elemental partitioning creates a refined intermetallic network and localized compositional gradients.
Redistribution stabilizes intermetallic phases enriched in oxidation-resistant elements.
Annealing-induced reordering causes selective enrichment at the alloy surface and grain boundaries.
The enriched microstructure promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide scale during high-temperature exposure.
The proposed protective scale comprises Al2O3, MgO, and possibly Gd oxides.
The refined and compositionally partitioned microstructure minimizes localized micro-galvanic coupling.
Reduced micro-galvanic coupling decreases localized corrosion attack.
Passive-film formation can improve corrosion resistance in Mg-rich compositionally complex alloys.
The initial Mg–Al–Cu–Zn–Gd alloy has an overall density below 6 g/cm3.
Annealing at approximately 550°C permits limited diffusion without bringing the alloy to full equilibrium.
The annealed alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the as-cast alloy in 0.1 M NaCl at room temperature.
The annealed alloy will develop an oxide scale with better adhesion and integrity than the as-cast alloy during oxidation at 800–900°C.
Post-annealing microscopy will reveal a refined intermetallic network.
Post-annealing characterization will reveal Al- and Gd-enriched regions at critical interfaces.
Differences in constituent properties favor stable intermetallic-compound formation under the stated boundary conditions.
Excessive homogenization or overly rapid diffusion would erase beneficial segregation and invalidate the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome only requires a lower corrosion current density, whereas the falsification rule requires a greater than 20% reduction. A smaller but statistically significant reduction could therefore satisfy the prediction while simultaneously falsifying the hypothesis.
